title: Ajamila calls his son
hook: a name read wrong at rehearsal, a dying man calling his son, and why so many Hindu children carry a god's name
carry: god's name reaches god, even called to a child
tomorrow: how can a puff of air on your palm change a whole word?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tyagaraja sang to Rama instead of the king: nada upasana, music itself can be worship. Today, the sound we hear more than any other: a name.

Roll call on the first day of anything. A name gets read off the list, and it comes out squashed, or stretched in the wrong places. Some people correct it every time. Some give up and answer to the wrong name for years. It can feel small and still sting. Hindu tradition says a name can matter more than anyone in the room knows. Here's the story it tells.
screen: `ROLL CALL.` → `THE NAME COMES OUT WRONG.` → `IT MATTERS MORE THAN YOU KNOW.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, a man named Ajamila had thrown away nearly everything good in his life. He cheated, he stole, he left the family that loved him. But he adored his youngest son, a little boy named Narayana, one of the names of Vishnu. At eighty-eight, Ajamila lay dying, and he saw three fierce figures come for him with ropes: the messengers of Yama, lord of death. Terrified, he cried out for his boy. Narayana! At once, messengers of Vishnu appeared and stopped Yama's. He has said the Lord's name, they said. Even called out for a child, the name has done its work. Ajamila lived, and gave the rest of his life to devotion. The Bhagavata draws the lesson itself: God's name, said even in passing, even meaning something else, still reaches God. That's one reason so many Hindu children are named for gods: Krishna, Lakshmi, Ganesh, Durga, Shiva. Many families say it plainly: every time you call your child, you've said God's name. A name chosen at the namakarana, the naming rite, can be a prayer said a dozen times a day without anyone noticing. So a name isn't only a label. Said with care, it may be the most repeated prayer in the house.
screen: `AJAMILA LOSES HIS WAY.` · `HE CALLS HIS SON: NARAYANA!` · `THE NAME REACHES GOD ANYWAY.` · `CHILDREN NAMED FOR GODS.` · then, large: `A NAME CAN BE A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Say your own name slowly, and if you know what it means, let the meaning sit with it. Then say the name of someone you love, with care, as a small blessing. If you pray, end with one name of God, said the way Ajamila said it: as a call. Then rest with the breath.
The sounds: today, the sound of a name, and a god's name said every day without anyone noticing.
Your line: God's name reaches God, even called to a child. Every call can be a prayer. Rest easy.

howItsDone: Many Hindu families choose a god's name, or a name for one of a god's qualities, at the namakarana, the naming rite held in the days after birth, so the child is called by a holy name every day.
